title: "The merge deleted my code" — find out what really happened
summary: A function that existed last week is gone, and the blame points at a merge commit. Learn to diff a merge against each parent, prove where the code was dropped, and restore it.
concepts: diff a merge against each parent
mental_model: A merge commit has two parents and therefore two diffs. Code lost in a bad resolution shows up as removed against one parent and absent against the other — comparing both is how you prove it, and blame cannot.

write.content:
def total(items):
    return sum(i['price'] for i in items)

steps.title: Confirm the code is gone
steps.why: `apply_discount` is not in the working tree and not in HEAD. Before any investigation, establish exactly what is missing and where it should be.
commands: sh -c 'git grep apply_discount || echo "not in the working tree"'
steps.expect: No sign of the function, and a merge commit in recent history.

steps.title: Blame is no help here
steps.why: Blame reports who last touched the lines that exist. A line that was deleted has nothing to blame — this is the specific failure mode that sends people to `git log -S`.
steps.expect: Blame shows only surviving lines; the pickaxe finds the commit that introduced the function.

steps.title: Find where the function lived and died
steps.why: `log -S` searches every commit's content. `--all` covers the feature branch too. Two results: the commit that added it, and the merge that lost it.
steps.expect: The discount commit on the branch, and the merge on main.

verify.label: the pickaxe found where the function existed

steps.title: Diff the merge against each parent
steps.why: This is the key move. `<merge>^1` is main before the merge, `<merge>^2` is the branch. Against parent 2 the function shows as REMOVED — proof the merge dropped it rather than never having it.
commands: sh -c 'merge=$(git log --merges -1 --format=%H); echo merge=$merge; git diff $merge^1 $merge -- billing.py'
steps.expect: Against parent 1: tax and rounding kept. Against parent 2: apply_discount removed with a minus sign.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'merge=$(git log --merges -1 --format=%H); git diff $merge^2 $merge -- billing.py | grep -c "^-.*apply_discount"'
verify.label: the merge removed the function relative to the branch it merged

steps.title: Read the merge the way git shows it by default
steps.why: `git show <merge>` prints a combined diff, which shows only hunks that differ from BOTH parents — precisely the lines a resolution changed. It is the fastest way to review a merge resolution, and almost nobody knows it exists.
steps.expect: The combined diff highlighting exactly what the resolver dropped.

steps.title: Recover the function from the parent
steps.why: The branch's version is still in history — the merge did not delete the commit, only its content in the result. Read the file from parent 2 and put the function back.
steps.expect: The original file, complete with apply_discount.

steps.title: Restore it properly and prove the fix
steps.why: Write the union of both sides: main's rounding and tax, plus the branch's discount function. Then confirm the pickaxe finds it in HEAD, so the next person does not repeat this investigation.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "Restore apply_discount, lost in the discounts merge resolution"

verify.label: both sides' code is present now
verify.hint: restore the function from <merge>^2 and keep main's changes too

verify.label: the lost function is restored alongside main's work
the pickaxe now finds it on main
the recovery commit explains what happened, for the next reader
the bad merge is still in history — you fixed forward, did not rewrite

pitfalls: `git log` and `git blame` hide merge diffs by default, which is why lost code looks like it vanished without a commit. `--diff-merges` or diffing against each parent reveals it.
`<merge>^1` is the branch merged INTO, `^2` is the branch merged FROM. Getting them the wrong way round inverts your conclusion entirely.
The commonest cause is resolving a conflict by taking one whole side — `git checkout --ours <file>` on a file where both sides had real changes.
Reviewing merge commits with `git show --cc` before pushing catches this class of mistake in seconds.
Turning on `merge.conflictStyle zdiff3` makes the base visible during resolution, which is the best prevention available.
